title: Someone dared the punishment to come.
subtitle: Mocking a warning instead of heeding it
then: In Makkah the deniers laughed at the warning of the Last Day. Some went as far as praying: {trap}if this is the truth, rain stones down on us.{/trap} The surah opens by naming that dare and answering it: {idea}the punishment is real and on its way.{/idea}
now: Someone at work jokes, "If God cared, He would have done something by now." Or you catch yourself thinking a warning does not apply since nothing has happened yet. {trap}Silence is not the same as safety.{/trap}
old: If nothing bad has happened yet, the warning was probably exaggerated.
new: A delay is not a denial. What is promised is already on its way.
try: Think of one warning you have been brushing off. Take it seriously for five minutes today.

title: When it comes, nobody can push it back.
subtitle: No one stands between the denier and the Day
then: The deniers of Quraysh trusted their clans and their wealth to protect them from anything. Ibn Kathir explains the verse plainly: {trap}no one can repel it if Allah wants it to happen.{/trap} The usual shields of Makkah would not work here.
now: You know how to get out of most things: a phone call, a favour, a good lawyer, the right excuse. That skill makes you feel untouchable. {idea}Some doors cannot be talked open.{/idea} The time to prepare is before you reach them.
old: There is always someone who can get me out of trouble.
new: Before Allah's decree, my connections and excuses carry no weight.
try: Notice one area where you rely on talking your way out. Choose honesty there today.

title: It comes from the Lord of the ways up.
subtitle: Who stands behind the warning

row.title: Allah
sub: owner of the ways of ascent

then: The deniers spoke as if the warning were just Muhammad's ﷺ idea. This verse names the source. Ibn Abbas said the ways of ascent mean {idea}loftiness and abundance{/idea}, and Mujahid said they are {idea}the ways of rising into the heavens.{/idea}
now: A notice from a friend you can ignore. A letter from the court you cannot. You open it differently because of who sent it. {idea}The Quran is a message from the One above everything{/idea}, and it reads differently when you remember that.
old: A reminder is only as serious as the person reading it to me.
new: The weight of the message comes from the One who sent it.
try: Before you read Quran next, pause and say: this is from my Lord. Then read.

title: A Day as long as fifty thousand years.
subtitle: The length of the Day of Judgement

sub: years, the measure of that Day

row.title: endless
sub: for those who withheld and denied

then: Ibn Abbas and others said this Day is the Day of Judgement. Ibn Kathir cites a hadith about the wealthy who {trap}did not give the due on their wealth{/trap}, standing through a Day of fifty thousand years until judgement is passed. The length is felt by those who denied.
now: A five-minute wait at the doctor's feels like an hour when you are scared. A long dinner with friends flies by. {idea}Time stretches with how you arrive.{/idea} What you do with your wealth and hours now shapes how long that Day will feel.
old: Judgement is one quick moment at the end.
new: That Day is long, and how it feels depends on what I bring to it.
try: Give something small today from what you have, even if no one asks.

title: Be patient, and make it beautiful.
subtitle: Patience without bitterness while being mocked
then: Ibn Kathir says this was addressed to the Prophet ﷺ: {idea}be patient with your people's rejection{/idea} and with their demand to hurry the punishment, since they thought it would never come. He was not told to argue harder. He was told to wait well.
now: A relative keeps mocking your prayer at family dinners. A colleague rolls their eyes every time you decline the drinks. You can stay quiet and stew, or you can stay kind. {idea}Beautiful patience keeps your heart clean while you wait.{/idea}
old: Being patient means swallowing it and resenting them quietly.
new: Real patience is calm and trusting, with no grudge hidden inside it.
try: The next time someone needles you today, answer once, kindly, and let it go.

title: They see it as far away.
subtitle: The comfort of thinking the end is distant
then: Ibn Kathir explains that the word for far, {trap}ba'id{/trap}, here means something they thought impossible. The deniers of Makkah did not just think the Hour was late. {trap}They thought it would never come.{/trap}
now: You plan to fix your prayer when life calms down. To call your mother when work slows. To repent after this phase. {trap}Far away is a comfortable place to keep things.{/trap} It quietly turns later into never.
old: There is plenty of time before any of this matters.
new: Thinking it is far away is exactly how people end up unready.
try: Pick one thing you keep saying you will do later. Do the first small step today.

title: But We see it near.
subtitle: Allah's view of time versus ours
then: Right after their view comes Allah's. Ibn Kathir notes that believers held its coming to be near, {idea}even though no one knows its time except Allah.{/idea} {idea}Whatever is approaching is near{/idea}, and it will surely happen.
now: Your phone says your next birthday is months away. Then it arrives, and the last year feels like a week. Every deadline you ever had felt far until it did not. {idea}Near is the honest word.{/idea}
old: The end is so far away it hardly affects my choices today.
new: Anything certain to come is already close.
try: Tonight, spend two minutes thinking: if it were near, what would I change first?

title: The sky will look like murky oil.
subtitle: The ceiling of the world melting
then: The surah now describes the Day the deniers mocked. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others said the sky will be {trap}like the residue of oil.{/trap} The most stable thing anyone in Makkah could point to would lose its form.
now: You look up from the bus stop and the sky is just there, like it always has been. You build your life assuming the backdrop stays fixed. {idea}Even the backdrop has an end date.{/idea}
old: Some things in this world are permanent.
new: Nothing here is fixed. Even the sky will change.
try: Look up at the sky once today and remember it will not always look like this.

title: Mountains will float like fluffed wool.
subtitle: The heaviest things made light
then: Mujahid, Qatadah and As-Suddi said the mountains will be {trap}like fluffed wool{/trap}, as another verse calls it carded wool. For people who lived among the mountains of Makkah, nothing seemed more permanent.
now: The house you are paying off. The career you built for fifteen years. The body you trust to carry you. They feel like mountains. {idea}They are real, and they are not forever.{/idea}
old: The big, solid parts of my life will always hold me up.
new: Even mountains drift on that Day. Only what I did for Allah stays.
try: Name one solid thing you lean on. Thank Allah for it out loud.

title: No close friend will ask about a friend.
subtitle: When everyone is consumed with themselves

row.title: they are drowning too
sub: each has enough of his own

then: Ibn Kathir says no close friend will ask about his friend {trap}while he sees him in the worst of conditions.{/trap} He will be worried about himself. He links it to the verse: every man that Day will have enough to make him careless of others.
now: Think of the friend you call first in a crisis, the one in every family group chat who always replies. On that Day they will be facing their own record. {idea}The friendships worth having are the ones that help you prepare now.{/idea}
old: My people will have my back no matter what.
new: On that Day each person faces their own load. Help each other now, while it counts.
try: Send one friend a message today that reminds them of Allah, kindly.

title: He would hand over his own children to escape.
subtitle: The ransom no one expects to offer

row.title: I would die for my kids

then: They will be made to see one another, yet flee. Ibn Kathir says even the child {trap}dearer to him than the last beat of his heart{/trap} he would wish to offer as ransom when he sees the horrors. {trap}Even that would not be accepted.{/trap}
now: You hold your child at the school gate and feel you would give anything for them. That love is real. The verse shows how far terror on that Day goes. {idea}The best protection for your family is the faith you build with them today.{/idea}
old: Nothing could ever make me turn on the people I love.
new: That Day's fear is beyond anything I know. Preparing now is the real love.
try: Pray one prayer today with your family or child beside you.

title: His wife and his brother join the offer.
subtitle: The ransom list keeps growing
then: The list continues: his wife, then his brother. Ibn Kathir pairs this with the verse that {trap}a heavily laden soul calls another to carry its load{/trap}, and nothing is lifted, even by close kin.
now: Your brother covers for you with your parents. Your spouse handles the bills you forget. You lean on them for so much. {idea}On that Day, nobody can carry your deeds for you.{/idea}
old: My family will share whatever I end up facing.
new: Each person carries their own record. I should carry mine well.
try: Do one task today you usually leave for your spouse or sibling.

title: Even the clan that sheltered him.
subtitle: The tribe that always protected him
then: In Makkah the clan was everything. It protected you, fed you, avenged you. Mujahid and As-Suddi said fasilah means {idea}his tribe and his kin{/idea}. Ibn Kathir cites the verse that when the Trumpet is blown, {trap}there will be no kinship among them.{/trap}
now: Your surname opens doors. Your family's name gets you hired, forgiven, welcomed. That shelter is a gift. {trap}It does not carry over.{/trap} What carries over is how you used it.
old: Where I come from and who my family is will protect me.
new: The shelter of family ends at that Day. Only my deeds go further.
try: Use your family's name or connections today to help someone who has none.

title: He would give the whole earth to be saved.
subtitle: The biggest ransom imaginable
then: The offer reaches its limit. Ibn Kathir says {trap}no ransom will be accepted{/trap}, even if he brought all the people of the earth and enough gold to fill it. The deniers of Makkah trusted wealth. Here it is worth nothing.
now: Payday comes, and for a moment you feel secure. Insurance, savings, an emergency fund. These are wise here. {idea}None of it is currency on that Day.{/idea} The only thing that crosses is what you did.
old: With enough money, I can fix almost anything.
new: All the wealth of the earth cannot buy one soul out of that Day.
try: Give a small charity today, quietly, as a deposit for the Day.

title: No. It is the Flame.
subtitle: The bargaining is cut off
then: After all the offers, one word: {trap}No!{/trap} Ibn Kathir says Allah is describing the Fire and {trap}the severity of its heat.{/trap} The criminal's bargaining ends there. The time for making deals was in this life.
now: You have probably said it: I will sort it out with Allah later. As if there will be a meeting where you can explain. {idea}The meeting is now.{/idea} Every prayer, every apology, every time you turn back is the negotiation.
old: When the time comes, I will find a way to make things right.
new: The way to make things right is open today, and only today is promised.
try: Make one sincere istighfar today for a specific thing, naming it to Allah.

title: A fire that strips away what we showed off.
subtitle: The Flame takes the face people saw
then: Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said the word refers to the skin of the head, and Al-Hasan said {trap}the honoured parts of the face.{/trap} The deniers of Makkah guarded their standing and dignity above all. The verse says the Fire removes exactly that.
now: You spend twenty minutes picking a profile photo. You rehearse how to come across in the meeting. None of that is wrong. But {idea}the outside is the part that does not last.{/idea} What you are inside is what you take with you.
old: How I look to people is what matters most about me.
new: The face I show the world is the first thing to go. The heart is what remains.
try: Do one good deed today that nobody will see or know about.

title: It calls the one who turned his back.
subtitle: Who the Fire recognises as its own

row.title: the Flame
sub: by name, it picks him out

then: Ibn Kathir says the Fire will call out on that Day and pick out its people {trap}as birds pick seeds.{/trap} They are the ones who {trap}denied with their hearts and abandoned deeds with their limbs.{/trap} Turning away has two parts: belief and action.
now: You do not say you reject anything. You just skip the prayer, mute the reminder, scroll past the lecture your friend sent. {idea}Turning away is often quiet.{/idea} It happens one ignored call at a time.
old: As long as I believe in my heart, what I do does not matter much.
new: Turning away happens in the heart and in the hands. Turning back does too.
try: Open the one reminder you have been scrolling past and read it fully.

title: He gathered and he hoarded.
subtitle: Wealth piled up and kept from its due

row.title: giving opens doors
sub: hold back, and Allah holds back

then: Ibn Kathir explains: he gathered wealth, piled it up, and {trap}refused to give Allah's right due on it.{/trap} He cites the Prophet's ﷺ words: {idea}do not hold back, or Allah will hold back from you.{/idea} In Makkah, wealth was the mark of a great man.
now: Your savings app shows a number you are proud of. A friend asks for help and you say things are tight. {trap}Saving is wise. Sitting on it while others need it is something else.{/trap}
old: What I earned is mine to keep, and giving is optional.
new: Part of what I hold belongs to others. Holding it back closes doors on me.
try: Look at your last payday. Set aside one small amount for someone in need.

title: People were created anxious.
subtitle: An honest description of human nature
then: After describing the deniers, the surah turns to human nature in general. Ibn Kathir says Allah {trap}informs about man and his inclination{/trap} to slip in his behaviour. The next verses explain what this anxiety looks like, and who is the exception.
now: You check your bank balance three times a day. You refresh the test results page. You lie awake replaying a conversation. {idea}This verse is not judging you. It is describing you{/idea}, so you can see the way out it offers next.
old: My restlessness means I am weak or failing.
new: Restlessness is part of being human. Allah names it, then shows the remedy.
try: The next time you feel anxious today, name it to yourself: this is human. Then breathe.

title: When harm touches him, he panics.
subtitle: Despair at the first sign of trouble
then: Ibn Kathir says when harm touches him he becomes frightened and worried, taken over {trap}by his despair that he will receive any good after it.{/trap} He cites the hadith that the worst thing in a man is {trap}greedy impatience and unrestrained cowardice.{/trap}
now: The email from HR. The scan result. The rent going up. Your mind leaps straight to the worst ending and stays there. {idea}The panic is not the problem. The despair underneath it is.{/idea}
old: When something goes wrong, it means everything is falling apart.
new: Harm is real but not final. Despair is the part I can let go of.
try: Write down one hard thing in your life now, and one past hardship that eased.

title: When good touches him, he holds it tight.
subtitle: Stinginess as the other side of anxiety
then: The same anxious person, now in good times. Ibn Kathir says if he gets a blessing from Allah {trap}he is stingy with it, not sharing it with others{/trap}, and withholds Allah's right in it. Panic and stinginess grow from the same fear.
now: The bonus lands and your first thought is what it can protect you from, not who it could help. {idea}The same worry that panics in hard times grips tight in good ones.{/idea}
old: When things go well, I need to protect what I got.
new: Clutching in good times is the same fear as panicking in bad ones.
try: When something good comes your way today, share a piece of it with someone.

title: Except those who pray.
subtitle: The exception to the anxious nature
then: Ibn Kathir says man is described with these faults {idea}except those whom Allah protects, helps and guides to good{/idea}, and these are the people who pray. The first remedy named for human anxiety is the prayer.
now: You have tried apps, podcasts, journaling, cold showers. Some help. But five times a day you are offered a break where you stand before the One who holds every outcome. {idea}The cure is already in your schedule.{/idea}
old: My anxiety needs a solution I have not found yet.
new: Prayer is where the anxious heart is steadied, five times a day.
try: In your next prayer, slow down in one sujood and tell Allah what worries you.

title: Their prayer is steady and constant.
subtitle: Not perfect prayer, consistent prayer
then: Ibn Kathir gives several meanings: guarding prayer's times, {idea}stillness and focus in it{/idea}, and keeping it up without breaks. He cites the hadith that {reward}the most beloved deeds to Allah are the most consistent, even if few.{/reward}
now: Ramadan you pray every night. Then a busy month at work and it fades. Or you rush through the movements while your mind plans dinner. {idea}Constant means both: every day, and actually present.{/idea}
old: I need to pray more intensely to make up for missed days.
new: Steady, calm, and regular beats rare and intense.
try: Pick one prayer you often rush. Pray it today slowly, letting each position settle.

title: Their wealth has a known share for others.
subtitle: Giving planned in advance, not by mood

row.title: a known right
sub: a set portion for the needy

row.title: give if I feel like it

then: Ibn Kathir explains that in their wealth there is {idea}a determined portion for those in need.{/idea} This is the cure for the stingy grip of verse 21. The giver does not wait for a feeling. The share is already counted.
now: Your salary comes in and the rent, phone bill and savings come out automatically. What if giving had its own line too, set before you spend? {idea}Known means planned.{/idea}
old: I will give when I have some extra left over.
new: A known part of my money already belongs to those in need.
try: Set up one small regular donation, even a tiny amount, today.

title: For the one who asks and the one who cannot.
subtitle: Two kinds of people in need
then: The known right goes to two people. One is {idea}the one who asks{/idea}, whose need you can see. The other is {idea}the deprived{/idea}, who does not or cannot ask. The believers in this passage look for both.
now: The man at the traffic light with a sign. And the coworker who quietly skips lunch every day near the end of the month. {idea}One asks. One never will.{/idea} Both are in the verse.
old: If someone really needed help, they would ask me.
new: Some of the most in need never ask. Part of giving is noticing.
try: Think of someone around you who may be struggling quietly. Help them without making it awkward.

title: They are sure the Day of Recompense is real.
subtitle: Belief that changes how you act
then: Ibn Kathir says they are sure of the Return, the Reckoning and the Recompense. {idea}Therefore they act like someone who hopes for reward and fears punishment.{/idea} This is the opposite of the deniers at the start of the surah, who saw the Day as far off.
now: If you knew your manager would review every message you sent this month, you would write differently. {idea}Believing in the Day works the same way.{/idea} It is less a statement and more a way of living.
old: I believe in the Day of Judgement, and that is enough.
new: Real belief in the Day shows up in how I act on an ordinary Tuesday.
try: Before one decision today, ask: how would this look on the Day?

title: They are wary of their Lord's punishment.
subtitle: Healthy fear that keeps you careful
then: The surah began with deniers who asked for the punishment to hurry. Here the believers are the reverse: {idea}fearful and dreadful{/idea}, as Ibn Kathir puts it. They do good and still do not feel they have earned safety.
now: The best surgeon still double-checks before the first cut. The safest driver still checks the mirror. {idea}Carefulness is not weakness. It is what keeps you safe.{/idea}
old: If I am doing good, I do not need to worry about punishment.
new: Doing good and staying careful go together.
try: Ask Allah today for protection from the Fire, by name, once.

title: No one can feel safe from it.
subtitle: Why the believers stay careful
then: Ibn Kathir says {trap}no one is safe from it{/trap} among those who understand Allah's command, {reward}except through the security of Allah Himself.{/reward} This is why the believers in verse 27 stay fearful even while they pray and give.
now: You have prayed for years, you give, people call you religious. It is easy to feel your place is secured. {idea}Safety is a gift you keep asking for, not a badge you already hold.{/idea}
old: I have done enough good to feel secure.
new: My safety rests on Allah's mercy, so I keep asking for it.
try: End one prayer today with a dua asking Allah to keep you steady until you meet Him.

title: They guard their chastity.
subtitle: Protecting the body as a trust
then: The list of believers' qualities continues. Ibn Kathir says they {idea}keep their private parts away from what is forbidden{/idea} and within what Allah has allowed. He notes this matches the opening of Surat Al-Mu'minun.
now: It starts small: a search late at night, a message that goes a bit too far, a show you keep watching. {idea}Guarding means stopping earlier than the line{/idea}, at the first door, not the last.
old: As long as I do not cross the final line, I am fine.
new: Guarding chastity means protecting it well before the line.
try: Remove one app, account, or habit that keeps leading you close to the line.

title: Within what Allah made lawful, there is no blame.
subtitle: Desire has an honoured place
then: The verse makes an exception to guarding: with their spouses, and what was lawful in that time, {idea}they are not to be blamed.{/idea} Ibn Kathir notes this was explained at the opening of Surat Al-Mu'minun. Islam does not treat desire as dirty. It gives it a home.
now: Some people grow up thinking any desire is shameful. Others think every desire should be followed. {idea}The verse sits between: not blamed within its place.{/idea} Your marriage, or the one you hope for, is part of your worship.
old: Wanting closeness is something to feel guilty about.
new: Desire within what Allah allows carries no blame. It can even be good.
try: If you are married, do one kind thing for your spouse today with the intention of pleasing Allah.

title: Seeking beyond the limit is trespassing.
subtitle: When desire crosses the boundary Allah set
then: After naming the lawful place for desire, the verse closes the door on everything past it: {trap}whoever seeks beyond that, they are the transgressors.{/trap} Ibn Kathir refers to the same passage at the start of Surat Al-Mu'minun.
now: Trespassing rarely starts with a big leap. It is one more message, one more click, one more late conversation. {idea}A fence is easiest to respect from a few steps back.{/idea}
old: Going a little past the line is not really crossing it.
new: Any step past the line Allah drew is trespassing, however small.
try: Identify the earliest step that usually leads you past a line. Avoid just that step today.

title: They keep their trusts and their promises.
subtitle: Reliability as a sign of faith
then: Ibn Kathir says when they are trusted they do not deceive, and {idea}when they make a covenant they do not break it.{/idea} He contrasts this with the hadith on the signs of a hypocrite: {trap}he lies, breaks promises, and betrays trust.{/trap}
now: You said you would call back. You told your friend their secret was safe. You promised your kid you would come to the match. {idea}Faith shows up in whether people can rely on you.{/idea}
old: Small promises and favours are not a religious matter.
new: Keeping my word, even in small things, is part of my faith.
try: Keep one small promise today that you were tempted to let slide.

title: They stand firm on what they witnessed.
subtitle: Honest testimony, without adding or hiding
then: Ibn Kathir says they guard their testimonies: {idea}they do not add or decrease{/idea}, nor do they conceal. He cites the verse: {trap}whoever hides it, his heart is sinful.{/trap}
now: Your colleague is blamed for a mistake you saw someone else make. A family argument needs someone to say what really happened. {idea}Staying quiet feels safe, but the truth needs a witness.{/idea}
old: Telling what I saw would only cause trouble for me.
new: Standing by the truth I witnessed is a trust, even when it costs me.
try: When you retell a story today, tell it exactly, with no extra spin.

title: They guard their prayer.
subtitle: The list opens and closes with prayer
then: Ibn Kathir notes that Allah {idea}begins this list with prayer and ends it with prayer{/idea}, which shows its importance. Here guarding means keeping its times, its pillars, its obligations and its recommended parts.
now: Prayer is the frame around everything else. When it is guarded, the honesty, the giving and the self-control have something to hold onto. {idea}When it slips, the rest usually follows.{/idea}
old: Prayer is one item on my list of good things to do.
new: Prayer is the frame that holds every other good quality in place.
try: Set an alarm for the one prayer you most often miss or delay.

title: In gardens, and honoured.
subtitle: Where the steady, honest people end up
then: After the long list, the reward. Ibn Kathir says they will be {reward}honoured with various types of pleasures and delights.{/reward} The surah contrasts this with the deniers who will be covered in humiliation at its end.
now: Nobody notices you praying on time in the office stairwell, or returning the extra change at the till. {reward}On that Day, those quiet habits are met with honour.{/reward}
old: Quiet, steady goodness goes unnoticed and unrewarded.
new: The quiet faithful are the ones who will be honoured guests.
try: Thank Allah for one good habit He has helped you keep.

title: Why do they rush away from you?
subtitle: Fleeing from the one bringing guidance
then: Ibn Kathir says these were people who saw the Prophet ﷺ and his signs, {trap}then fled from him, group by group.{/trap} He compares them to the verse about wild donkeys {trap}fleeing from a lion.{/trap} Ibn Abbas said they stared at him and mocked.
now: A friend starts talking about prayer and you suddenly need to check your phone. A reminder appears and you swipe it away fast. {idea}Notice what you run from. It may be what you need.{/idea}
old: I walk away from reminders because they are not relevant to me.
new: The speed of my escape from a reminder can show how much I need it.
try: The next time you want to walk away from a reminder today, stay one minute longer.

title: In little groups, on the right and the left.
subtitle: Huddled circles that mock instead of listen
then: Ibn Abbas said they turned {trap}right and left away from him, mocking him.{/trap} The word means scattered groups. Ibn Kathir cites a hadith that the Prophet ﷺ came out to people sitting in circles and said: {idea}why do I see you in separate groups?{/idea}
now: A group chat that turns every serious topic into a meme. The table at work where the religious guy is always the joke. {trap}A circle can keep you comfortable and closed.{/trap}
old: Laughing along with my friends is harmless.
new: The group I sit with can shield me from the truth or open me to it.
try: Next time a reminder becomes a joke in your group, do not add to it.

title: Do they really expect the Garden?
subtitle: Hoping for Paradise while fleeing the path
then: Ibn Kathir asks the question the verse asks: {trap}is this their wish, yet they flee from the Messenger ﷺ in aversion to the truth?{/trap} They expected a good ending while turning their backs on its way.
now: You expect to pass the exam without studying. You expect your health to hold while ignoring the doctor. {idea}Hope is beautiful when it walks.{/idea} Wishing for Jannah while avoiding its road is something else.
old: Allah is merciful, so it will all work out in the end.
new: Real hope moves me toward the Garden, not just toward the wish.
try: Take one small step today toward the person you hope to be on that Day.

title: No. We made them from what they know.
subtitle: Remember the humble start
then: The deniers called resurrection far-fetched. Ibn Kathir says Allah answers by pointing to how they began: {idea}from despised water, as they themselves admit.{/idea} Bringing back is easier than making the first time.
now: Look at a baby scan on a friend's phone. A few weeks ago that was almost nothing. Now it has a heartbeat. {idea}The One who did that does not struggle to do it again.{/idea} And none of us began as anything to be proud of.
old: Coming back to life after death sounds impossible.
new: The One who made me from nothing can easily bring me back.
try: Look at your hand today and remember where it began. Say alhamdulillah.

title: By the Lord of every sunrise and sunset.
subtitle: An oath by the One who moves the stars
then: Ibn Kathir says this is the One who made east and west and {idea}subjected the stars, rising in the east and setting in the west.{/idea} The oath begins with a no, rejecting their claim. {idea}Creating the heavens is greater than creating people.{/idea}
now: Your commute home at sunset, the sky orange behind the buildings. Every day the sun rises at a slightly different point and sets at another. {idea}The One managing that is not troubled by bringing you back.{/idea}
old: Resurrection feels too big to really happen.
new: The One who runs every sunrise has no difficulty raising me again.
try: Watch one sunrise or sunset this week and think of this verse.

title: We can replace them with better, and no one outruns Us.
subtitle: No one is indispensable to Allah
then: Ibn Kathir gives two meanings. One: Allah will bring them back in {idea}better bodies than these.{/idea} Two, preferred by Ibn Jarir: {idea}a people who will obey and not disobey.{/idea} Either way, {trap}Allah is not unable.{/trap}
now: You volunteer at the mosque and start to feel the place would fall apart without you. You skip it for a month and it runs fine. {idea}Serving is an honour Allah gives, not a favour you do Him.{/idea}
old: If I step back, the good work will suffer.
new: Allah can always bring better people. Serving is my privilege, not His need.
try: Do one act of service today and thank Allah for choosing you for it.

title: Leave them to their idle talk and games.
subtitle: Not every argument needs winning
then: Ibn Kathir says this addresses the Prophet ﷺ: {idea}leave them in their denial and stubbornness{/idea}, until they meet their Day. The introduction says he was being consoled: do not take their mockery to heart.
now: The comment section where someone mocks your faith. The cousin who wants to debate at every wedding. You do not have to win. {idea}Say your piece once, kindly, and step back.{/idea}
old: If I do not respond to every mockery, I am letting it win.
new: Some talk is just play. I can leave it and trust the Day to settle it.
try: Skip one argument online today that would only feed idle talk.

title: Out of the graves, rushing as if to a flag.
subtitle: The Day they rush to the reckoning
then: Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said they rush {trap}as if towards a flag.{/trap} In another reading the word means an idol, so they rush the way they once {trap}hurried to touch their idols{/trap}, each wanting to be first.
now: Think of what you rush toward: the sale, the new phone release, the notification. {idea}What we rush toward in this life says a lot about us.{/idea} One day everyone will rush toward one place.
old: What I chase every day is harmless and does not define me.
new: What I rush toward now is a preview of what I am living for.
try: Notice the first thing you rush to check tomorrow morning. Put prayer before it.

title: Eyes lowered. This is the Day they were promised.
subtitle: The surah ends where it began
then: Ibn Kathir says their eyes are humbled and humiliation covers them {trap}in return for how they behaved arrogantly in the world{/trap} by refusing to obey. The surah opened with a man daring the punishment to come. {trap}It closes with: this is the Day you were promised.{/trap}
now: Lowering your eyes in prayer is a choice today. Lowering your pride in an apology is a choice today. {idea}Humility chosen now is honour later.{/idea}
old: Backing down or humbling myself makes me look weak.
new: Humbling myself before Allah now spares me humiliation on that Day.
try: In your next sujood, stay a little longer and let your pride rest on the floor.
